items.s: A holder of 100 shares with three seats open may cast at most 100 votes for any one nominee.
items.w: Statutory voting limits the holder to one vote per share for each seat, so votes cannot be stacked.

items.s: A holder of 100 shares with three seats open may cast all 300 of her votes for a single nominee.
items.w: Cumulative voting pools shares times seats into one pot that can be placed on one candidate.

items.s: Each share votes once per seat, and votes may never be combined onto one director.
items.w: Under statutory voting each seat is a separate vote of one vote per share.

items.s: The shareholder pools her total votes and may split them, such as 15 for one candidate and 5 for another.
items.w: Cumulative voting lets the holder allocate the pooled votes in any manner she chooses.

items.s: A holder of 200 shares and five open seats can never give one nominee more than 200 votes.
items.w: Statutory voting caps the votes for any one nominee at the number of shares owned.

items.s: A holder of 200 shares and five open seats has a total pool of 1,000 votes to allocate.
items.w: The cumulative pool equals shares times open seats, here 200 times 5, which is 1,000 votes.

items.s: With 10 shares and two seats, the holder may cast 10 votes for each of two directors but not 20 for one.
items.w: Statutory voting allows up to 10 votes for each seat and forbids moving votes between seats.

items.s: The exercise price is set below the current market value of the stock.
items.w: Rights are sold at a discount, which is why they have value and trade separately.

items.s: The exercise price is set above the stock’s market price when issued, so there is no intrinsic value at issue.
items.w: Warrants are generally issued out of the money and become valuable only if the stock rises.

items.s: Short-term instrument; holders typically have 30 to 45 days to decide whether to exercise.
items.w: A rights offering gives shareholders a short window, typically 30 to 45 days, to exercise.

items.s: Long-term instrument that generally lasts five years or more.
items.w: Warrants typically remain outstanding much longer than rights, generally five years or more.

items.s: Lets existing shareholders keep their proportionate ownership when the company issues new shares.
items.w: Pre-emptive rights exist to prevent dilution by letting owners buy their pro rata share.

items.s: Attached to a bond or preferred stock as a sweetener so the issuer can pay a lower rate or dividend.
items.w: Warrants make another security more attractive, allowing the issuer to pay less interest or dividend.

items.s: Does not prevent dilution of existing shareholders when exercised.
items.w: Unlike pre-emptive rights, warrants are not designed to protect proportionate ownership against dilution.

items.s: Cannot be eliminated by spreading a portfolio across many different stocks.
items.w: Market risk hits nearly all securities together, so diversification does not remove it.

items.s: The best protection is diversification, so the investor does not put all eggs in one basket.
items.w: Company-specific risk is reduced by holding many issuers, since one failure is muted.

items.s: A product recall or management change at one single company.
items.w: Events affecting a single company are business or specific risk, not market-wide risk.

items.s: A recession or war that pushes down most stocks at the same time.
items.w: Recessions and wars are named sources of systematic risk affecting the whole market.

items.s: Can be hedged with derivatives such as options that create offsetting positions.
items.w: Though not diversifiable, market risk can be hedged with options to limit loss.

items.s: Also called business risk or specific risk because it generally will not hit the entire portfolio.
items.w: Non-systematic risk is called business or specific risk because it is limited to one company.

items.s: Interest rate changes that move prices across the entire market.
items.w: Interest rate changes are listed among the common sources of systematic risk.

items.s: The issuer may repurchase the shares at its discretion, and the investor must sell them back.
items.w: Callable preferred can be called by the issuing company, forcing the holder to sell.

items.s: The holder, not the issuer, chooses whether to exchange the shares for common stock at a fixed ratio.
items.w: Convertible preferred gives the investor the option to exchange into common stock.

items.s: Generally pays a higher dividend than non-callable preferred from the same issuer.
items.w: The higher dividend compensates the investor for the risk that the shares will be called.

items.s: Generally pays a lower dividend than nonconvertible preferred because it offers common stock upside.
items.w: Investors trade away dividend income for the upside potential of the common stock.

items.s: The company is likely to use this feature when interest rates fall and cheaper capital is available.
items.w: The issuer redeems when it can replace the shares with new ones paying a lower dividend.

items.s: A $100 par share exchangeable at $20 per common share has a conversion ratio of five.
items.w: The ratio is par divided by the conversion price, here 100 divided by 20, which equals five.

items.s: A feature that advantages the issuer rather than the investor.
items.w: Callable is the issuer-favorable feature, while convertible, cumulative and participating favor the investor.

items.s: Used by a company that believes its share price is too high to attract buyers.
items.w: Forward splits create more, lower-priced shares to make the stock look more affordable.

items.s: Used by an issuer whose $0.10 stock risks falling below the minimum price for exchange listing.
items.w: A reverse split lifts the price to help the issuer stay above the exchange minimum.

items.s: In a 2-for-1 split, the investor ends up with twice the shares at half the price.
items.w: A 2-for-1 forward split doubles the share count and halves the price, leaving value unchanged.

items.s: In a 1-for-5 split, five $4 shares become one $20 share.
items.w: A reverse split converts positions into proportionately fewer, higher-priced shares with no value change.

items.s: The investor’s per-share cost basis is adjusted upward.
items.w: With fewer shares representing the same total cost, the basis per share increases.

items.s: All open orders in the stock are cancelled when it occurs.
items.w: Anytime there is a reverse split, all open orders to trade the stock are cancelled.

items.s: Technically the same event as a stock dividend, such as a 10% dividend equaling an 11-for-10 split.
items.w: A forward split and a stock dividend both give extra shares at a proportionately lower price.

items.s: The trade settles one business day after the trade date (T + 1).
items.w: Regular way equity trades settle T + 1, meaning one business day after trade date.

items.s: Same-day payment and same-day settlement of the trade.
items.w: Cash settlement entails payment and delivery on the very day the trade is executed.

items.s: The ex-dividend date falls on the same day as the record date.
items.w: Because settlement takes one business day, regular way ex-date equals the record date.

items.s: The ex-dividend date is the business day after the record date.
items.w: A same-day settled trade on the record date still gets the dividend, so ex-date is the next day.

items.s: A buyer purchasing on the record date is too late and does not receive the dividend.
items.w: The trade settles after the record date, so the seller keeps the dividend.

items.s: A buyer purchasing on the record date settles that same day and does receive the dividend.
items.w: Same-day settlement puts the buyer on the books by the record date.

items.s: The way the majority of equity transactions settle.
items.w: Most equity trades settle regular way rather than through cash settlement.
